# Charter — S16 Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit (retrospective, 2026-11-28)

- **Project:** S16 'Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit', track v1, ADM phase G, delivery plateau, tranche 7
- **Delivered:** three tables (`inference_call`, `prompt_audit`, `prompt_audit_finding`) with row-level security forced; the engine capture seam that writes one row per external call inside the call's own transaction; and a prompt audit that is a procedure with one bounded model call, whose publish path refuses a high finding unless the author acknowledges it.
- **Authority:** the tranche-7 authorisation recorded by the tranche-6 review, exercised under the standing delegation 01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14.
- **Acceptance:** `acceptance/programme/S16.toml`, whose gate is that every model call becomes a durable, tenant-scoped row carrying the prompt's identity, the token counts and the provider's prompt-cache classes, so cost and cache are a query rather than a guess.
- **Closure:** the project is already closed in the record; this pack supplies the charter, baseline, artefact set, registers, contract, WBS deliverable, Phase-G review, outputs and closure review the row was closed without, then re-closes it through its own gate.

body.acceptance_criteria: The manifest's six requirements, each with its own check: the three tables exist with row-level security forced; a real external call's stored row matches the router's own usage field for field; the cache constraint refuses a hit with no read tokens; the audit is deterministic and only a high finding blocks a publish; no prompt action holds a process write; and the OpenAPI lock stays current.
body.assignment: Deliver the architectural record for an inference ledger: every model call the conveyor makes becomes a durable, tenant-scoped row carrying the prompt's identity, the token counts and both prompt-cache classes, with a prompt audit over the three prompt surfaces. The assignment is retrospective — the product shipped on 2026-11-09 and this statement records the architecture it was built to, not one requested in advance.
body.constraints: No new technology and no second writer: the engine seam is the only place a call is recorded, and a handler that wrote its own row would make the fact exist twice. Join keys stay integers without foreign keys because database-level referential integrity bypasses row-level security. The capture must never fail the call it is recording, which constrains it to the call's own transaction.
body.responsibilities: The programme architect authors the set under the standing delegation; the Architecture Board reviews it; the SRO is accountable for the cost-observability outcome; the platform engineer operates the capture seam and the ninety-day audit; the tenant admin consults on retention. The retrospective author is explicitly not the accepting role, so the separation of duties holds even though the same session wrote the product record.
body.retrospective: This statement is written after the fact and says so. Where the product's proof is narrower than the claim — the shipped capture test runs against a stub and the live-router rehearsal is still pending — the gap is recorded in the evidence output and in the risk register rather than smoothed into a pass. The Phase-G review's level reflects that distinction.
body.scope: In scope: the Phase A–D artefact set, the data entities, the capture seam, the audit procedure and the retention decision. Out of scope: any screen (S12 builds both), the inference router and the billing service (this project reads their usage, it does not replace them), a tenant-authored prompt store, AI-driven prompt repair, kata tables and any cadence configuration table.

# Solution Concept Diagram — S16 Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit (Phase A)

## Metadata

Type diagram; phase A; plateau psa; version 1; status draft; owner the programme architect (conveyor-e2e); reviewer the Architecture Board; review date 2026-11-28; project S16; tranche 7; retrospective under the standing delegation 01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14. This artefact is authored by the retrospective rework and does not attest contemporaneous intent.

## Entries

The concept has one seam. Every external call passes `invoke_external` in the engine, which records the call's row inside the same transaction, then returns the response whether or not the record succeeded. The audit is a procedure with one bounded model call that reads the prompt surfaces and writes findings, and the publish path refuses a high finding unless the author acknowledges it.

## Links

Realizes the Requirements Catalog; depends on the Business Capability Map and the Data Entity catalog for its two halves; reuses the engine seam and the action declaration pattern the platform already ships. The diagram is described in prose rather than as an image because the artefact store carries text bodies and a binary would be a second, unchecked source.

## Document

The concept deliberately has no second path: a handler that wrote its own ledger row would make the fact exist twice. The diagram therefore shows one writer, one table family and one reader, and the audit derives its findings from the same rows the ledger writes rather than from a parallel capture.

# Business Capability Map — S16 Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit (Phase B)

## Metadata

Type diagram; phase B; plateau hld; version 1; status draft; owner the programme architect (conveyor-e2e); reviewer the Architecture Board; review date 2026-11-28; project S16; tranche 7; retrospective under the standing delegation 01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14. This artefact is authored by the retrospective rework and does not attest contemporaneous intent.

## Entries

Three capabilities. Inference capture turns a call into a durable row and is the engine's, not a handler's. Prompt audit turns a prompt surface into findings and is a procedure. Cost attribution turns rows into an answer and is a read, never a write. Each capability names the action family it exposes and the requirement it satisfies.

## Links

Derives from the Solution Concept Diagram and the Requirements Catalog; feeds the Data Entity and Technology Standards catalogs. The capability view is the one the tenant sees: capture happens without the tenant asking, audit happens when a prompt is published, and attribution happens when someone asks what a run cost.

## Document

The map is a value view, not an org view: it says what the platform can do for a tenant, not which team owns it. That split matters here because capture is engine code while audit is a procedure, and a reader who confuses the two will look for a handler that records calls and not find one.

## Entries

Three data entities and their components. `inference_call` carries the prompt identity, the token counts, the cache classes and the cost context; `prompt_audit` carries the audit run and its prompt sha; `prompt_audit_finding` carries one finding with its severity and its determinism key. Join keys to `procedure`, `procedure_step`, `run_step` and `conversation_turn` are integers without foreign keys, deliberately.

Derives from the Business Capability Map; realizes the capture capability; depends on the Technology Standards catalog for the constraint and RLS conventions. The entities are tenant-scoped and carry row-level security forced, so the catalogue names the tenant column as a component of every entity rather than as a convention. The absent foreign keys are an integrity trade: referential integrity checked by the database bypasses row-level security, so an orphan join is possible and the report has to catch it.

input.body: The capture is written inside the call's own transaction so that it can never fail the call. The consequence is the mirror image: a genuine database failure rolls the audit row back with the rest of the transaction, and a call that happened leaves no ledger trace. The trade is deliberate but it is not free, and a silent under-count is harder to notice than a failed call.
input.response: Alert on a router call count that exceeds the ledger row count over a window, so the rollback case surfaces as a discrepancy rather than as an absence.
input.title: Capture shares the call's transaction, so a database failure can roll back the ledger row

input.body: The joins to `procedure`, `procedure_step`, `run_step` and `conversation_turn` are integers rather than foreign keys, because database-level referential integrity runs outside row-level security and would let one tenant's check read another's rows. An orphaned ledger row is therefore permitted by construction, and the grouping report is the only thing between the design and a silently unattributed cost.
input.response: Keep the report's group-by on the prompt sha, and treat an unattributed row count above zero as a finding rather than as noise.
input.title: Join keys carry no foreign keys, so an orphaned row is possible and only the report catches it

input.body: The cache status is derived from the response, never the request, and falls to `unknown` when the provider omits the class. That is the right call for honesty and the wrong one for a savings report: an under-reported cache benefit looks like a system that caches badly. The row is correct; the report needs to separate `unknown` from `miss` before anyone reads a trend from it.
input.response: Keep `unknown` as its own report bucket and refuse to fold it into `miss` in any downstream aggregate.

# Project Brief — S16 Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit (retrospective, 2026-11-28)

## Outcome

Every model call the conveyor makes becomes a durable, tenant-scoped row carrying the prompt's identity, the token counts and the provider's prompt-cache classes, and a prompt audit sits on the publish path — so what a run cost and whether it was cached is a query rather than a guess.

## Boundary

S16 owns the three ledger tables, the engine capture seam and the audit procedure. It does not own a screen (S12 builds both), the inference router or the billing service (their usage is read, not replaced), a tenant-authored prompt store, AI-driven prompt repair, kata tables or a cadence configuration table.

## Reuse sources

The engine seam `invoke_external` in `crates/actions/src/invoke.rs`, the action declaration pattern in `crates/actions/src/spec.rs`, the copilot system prompt in `crates/api/src/copilot/turns.rs`, the router's `Usage` schema, and the existing join targets `procedure`, `procedure_step`, `run_step` and `conversation_turn`.

## Inception units

Four: the Phase A set (stakeholders, drivers, requirements, concept), the Phase B capability map, the Phase C data entities and the Phase D standards. Each is one authored artefact in this pack and one reviewable unit for the Board.

## Dependencies

S02 and S03 supply the schema and the card model; S04 the registry and transport; S10 the conversation turn; S11 the procedure and step tables. S13 declares `captures_usage` when it lands, S12 builds the screens and S17 carries the two prune schedule rows.

`acceptance/programme/S16.toml` at the pinned snapshot. The gate is the ledger plus the audit; the field-for-field capture check and the determinism check are the two that cannot be satisfied by a stub, and the first of them is currently proved on a stub only.

## Capabilities

Three: inference capture (a call becomes a row), prompt audit (a prompt becomes findings) and cost attribution (rows become an answer). Only the third is a read; the first two are writes on paths that already exist.

The work is complete and the record is being supplied retrospectively. The operative order was schema, seam, audit, report; the remaining work is the live-router rehearsal, which is a proof rather than a build, and the two prune schedules, which are S17's.

# User stories — S16 Inference Ledger and Prompt Audit (retrospective, Phase G)

## Personas

An operator who must answer what a model call cost and whether it was cached, and an auditor who must prove which prompt produced a call and what the audit found. Both read the conveyor's own database, not a provider dashboard.

## Stories

- As an operator, I want every model call to be one durable, tenant-scoped row with token counts and both prompt-cache classes, so that cost is a query rather than a guess.
- As an auditor, I want the row to carry the prompt's identity, so that a cost line can be tied to the prompt version that produced it.
- As a release owner, I want a high prompt-audit finding to block the publish, so that an audited defect cannot ship behind a green build.

## Scenarios

S1 every call writes exactly one row through the engine's single seam; S2 both cache classes are recorded; S3 a high audit finding blocks the publish; S4 the report groups by prompt sha. The gate is the ledger and the blocking audit, not a dashboard.

`python3 scripts/rework-content-check.py --project S16 --content docs/evidence/rework/tranche-7/rework-content-S16.json --snapshot /tmp/snap-7/data --wsjf 9,7,9,8 --closes true`, then the factory run and the receipt assertion; the product check reads the ledger and audit groups from the pinned snapshot.

## Independent

The pack writes only S16's record rows against the pinned snapshot; its product is fully in-tree and its receipt is the cheapest of the three to make green. The other members share the snapshot and the cadence rows but no act of S16 depends on their products.

The pack supplies the record set the standard binds; the review (#755) and the promotion (#852) are owned elsewhere. The deferred live-router rehearsal is named as deferred, not negotiated away: the receipt's product check proves what is proved.

S16 is benefit `B5` (one model): a per-call ledger with prompt identity and cache classes turns model spend into a query. A green receipt is the evidence the tranche review needs to claim that, and the blocking audit is the control that keeps it honest.

The refinement record measures eight open record packages for S16 (0 P0, 8 P1): charter, baseline, contract, review, the seven A–D artefacts and the closure set. The factory journals every act, so an interrupted run resumes at the member it stopped on.

One pack, one factory run, one receipt, one closure; no product rebuild and no cluster change. The unit is one branch and one pull request.

Every claim has an executable check: the offline content checker at the pinned snapshot, the factory's post-write receipt with one row per manifest check, and the tranche exit gate that refuses a stale or red receipt.

S16 depends on S02, S03, S04, S10 and S11, all delivered and closed: the engine seam, the action registry, the run record and the surfaces that read the ledger. No dependency is outside a closed tranche.
